 When Safe Havens Boil: Gold, Silver and the Recovery Test by Amit Gupta, Kedia Advisory
 News By Tags | 
 #Gold 
 #CommodityTips 
 #ExpertViews 
 #Silver 
 #AmitGupta 
 #KediaAdvisory 
 - Gold’s 32% retreat and silver’s 62% collapse reflect changing monetary expectations.
 - Central-bank buying and renewed ETF inflows preserve gold’s strategic appeal.
 - A sustainable recovery requires softer oil, lower real yields and investment demand.
 Gold near $3,778 an ounce and silver around $46 on November 18 expose the scale of bullion’s reversal. Against January peaks near $5,599 and $121.65, respectively, the declines approach 32% and 62%. What began as profit-taking has become a test of whether investors can distinguish temporary financial stress from lasting fundamental damage.
 The familiar boiling-frog metaphor captures the behavioural trap: investors gradually normalise worsening conditions. Repeated buying opportunities encouraged confidence, even as leverage, technical breakdowns and changing interest-rate expectations transformed the market. January’s abrupt liquidation showed how quickly crowded positions could unravel.
 The subsequent energy shock complicated bullion’s safe-haven role. Expensive oil increased inflation risks, supporting higher bond yields and a stronger dollar. These forces raised the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing metals. By November 18, markets assigned a 96.7% probability to a December Federal Reserve increase of 25 basis points; a 50-point increase carried just 3.3%.
 Silver faced an additional industrial adjustment. The Silver Institute forecasts 2026 industrial consumption falling 3% to 640 million ounces, partly reflecting reduced silver usage and substitution in solar manufacturing. Yet non-solar industrial demand is expected to grow 4.5%. Mine production is projected to decline only 0.5% to 834 million ounces, leaving a 35-million-ounce deficit. The downturn therefore reflects investment pressures and changing consumption patterns alongside continuing supply constraints.
 Gold’s institutional foundations remain substantial. World Gold Council data show central banks purchased approximately 675 tonnes during January–September, including 321 tonnes in the third quarter. Global gold ETFs added 211.2 tonnes in Q3 after losing 47.3 tonnes in Q2. China’s central bank added 26 tonnes in October, extending its buying streak to 24 months. Reserve diversification remains supportive, although central-bank purchases alone cannot prevent further volatility or speculative selling.
 For Indian investors, currency movements add another layer. A strengthening rupee reduces the domestic value of dollar-denominated bullion. Illustratively, a 5% international price decline combined with a 2% fall in USD/INR produces approximately a 6.9% domestic decline before duties, premiums and other adjustments.
 History offers perspective, rather than a timetable. Kedia Advisory’s historical study records silver’s 60.3% collapse in 2008 followed by a 489.5% rally towards 2011. However, rebounds and full recoveries differ: after the 1980 crash, a 124.5% rebound still left silver below its previous peak.
 The next catalyst may come from energy. IEA reports North Sea Dated crude falling from $136 in early October to around $93, potentially easing inflation pressure. Conditional 2027 scenarios envisage gold at $4,640–$5,100 and silver at $72–$84, with $96.40 possible under stronger conditions. Downside reference supports remain $3,450 and $40.
 These targets require improving monetary conditions and sustained investment flows. Renewed inflation, dollar strength or geopolitical disruption could delay recovery. The boiling-frog lesson is to recognise changing conditions early: long-term conviction becomes more credible when oil, real yields and demand begin confirming it together.
